Package hadur2.core.physics

Class DiaUtils

java.lang.Object
hadur2.core.physics.DiaUtils
public final class DiaUtils extends Object
Small geometry and arithmetic helpers shared by the whole core: projecting points, bearings between points, bullet flight times, the orbit's acceleration sign, firing-angle grids and a Wald margin of error.

Conventions are Robocode's. Angles are radians with 0 north (+y) and growing clockwise, so moving length px along angle a adds sin(a) × length to x and cos(a) × length to y (sine and cosine swapped from the usual maths convention). absoluteBearing(Point2D.Double, Point2D.Double) is the inverse of project(Point2D.Double, double, double). Distances are in px, times in ticks.

Every method is a pure function, and only setBackAsFront(hadur2.core.model.BotOrders.Builder, double, double) touches the model (it writes into an order builder).

    • accel

      public static double accel(double velocity, double previousVelocity)
      A robot's acceleration relative to the way it was moving: positive when it speeds up in its direction of travel, negative when it brakes, whichever way it faces. A plain difference of velocities would call braking while reversing "acceleration". From a standstill any change counts as speeding up. Each wave records it as its target's acceleration, one of the KNN formulas' features.
      Parameters:
      velocity - this tick's velocity, in px/tick (signed: negative is reversing)
      previousVelocity - the previous tick's velocity, in px/tick
      Returns:
      the change in speed, in px/tick per tick

    • normalizeAngle

      public static double normalizeAngle(double angle, double reference)
      angle moved by whole turns until it is within π of reference, so two angles can be compared or ordered without a wrap-around between them. Used to put the ends of a bullet shadow and a bearing on the same side of the ±π seam.

      The loop steps one turn at a time, so it expects angles a few turns apart at most; an infinite angle never gets within π and would not return.

      Parameters:
      angle - the angle to move, in radians
      reference - the angle to move it near, in radians
      Returns:
      angle plus a whole number of turns, within π of reference

    • generateFiringAngles

      public static double[] generateFiringAngles(int numAngles, double maxEscapeAngle)
      numAngles firing angles spread evenly over [-maxEscapeAngle, maxEscapeAngle], relative to the head-on bearing, with the middle one at 0 (guess factor 0). Angle x is at guess factor (x - mid) / mid in [-1, 1]. numAngles should be odd and at least 3: an even count puts the last angle past the escape angle, and 1 divides by zero.
      Parameters:
      numAngles - how many angles, odd
      maxEscapeAngle - the escape angle the grid spans each way, in radians
      Returns:
      the angles, in radians, from -maxEscapeAngle up

    • generateFiringAngles

      public static double[] generateFiringAngles(int numAngles, double negativeEscapeAngle, double positiveEscapeAngle)
      GUN-3: numAngles firing angles spread evenly over [-negativeEscapeAngle, positiveEscapeAngle], relative to the head-on bearing. Unlike generateFiringAngles(int, double), the two sides need not be equal, so a target's precise escape angle (which the walls and its own heading can make asymmetric) is covered exactly rather than the smaller, symmetric classic one: the grid used to test only out to the classic maximum escape angle even though a neighbour's firing angle (from Wave.preciseEscapeAngle(boolean)) could fall outside it, which meant those neighbours could never be the chosen angle if the true best angle lay beyond the classic bound.
      Parameters:
      numAngles - how many angles, at least 2
      negativeEscapeAngle - the escape angle the grid spans on the negative side, radians
      positiveEscapeAngle - the escape angle the grid spans on the positive side, radians
      Returns:
      the angles, in radians, from -negativeEscapeAngle to positiveEscapeAngle, evenly spaced

    • marginOfError

      public static double marginOfError(double probability, int numDataPoints)
      The 95% margin of error of a proportion by the normal (Wald) approximation: 1.96 × sqrt(p (1 - p) / n). It is 0 for a rate of exactly 0 or 1 and undefined for n = 0, so it understates the doubt over few samples; the policies' inputs use Estimate's Agresti-Coull margin instead. The surf's hit-rate thresholds and the round statistics use this one.
      Parameters:
      probability - the observed rate, in [0, 1]
      numDataPoints - the number of trials
      Returns:
      the margin, as a rate

    • setBackAsFront

      public static void setBackAsFront(BotOrders.Builder orders, double heading, double goAngle)
      Drives toward goAngle, reversing instead of turning more than 90 degrees. Writes the body turn and distance into orders.

      A Robocode robot drives equally fast backwards, so any heading is at most a quarter turn from either its front or its back. Turning the short way and driving the matching way keeps the robot's turn (and the speed it loses to turn rate, see Rules.getTurnRate(double)) small. The 100 px distance only has to be larger than the robot can cover before the next order replaces it.

      Parameters:
      orders - the orders to write the body turn (radians, positive clockwise) and the distance (px, negative for reverse) into
      heading - the robot's current body heading, in radians
      goAngle - the direction to move in, in radians
